Configures chameleon-rs for the whole process: where templates loaded by name live, for

Chameleon templates, modernized: a Rust engine that runs Chameleon templates unchanged, several times faster, with async rendering and built-in framework integrations.
Chameleon templates, modernized. Several times faster.
chameleon-rs is Chameleon’s template language on a new engine written in Rust. Your existing templates and code run unchanged, with byte-identical output, several times faster. It also adds what a modern Python web app expects: async rendering that never blocks the event loop, built-in integrations for Flask/Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, Robyn and Litestar, partials, Markdown, and support for free-threaded Python. No runtime dependencies.

title: chameleon-rs
text:
Install
uv pip install chameleon-rs
CPython 3.12 to 3.15, including the free-threaded builds (3.14t, 3.15t). The wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows include the compiled engine, so you don’t need a Rust toolchain, and stock Chameleon doesn’t need to be installed.

title: chameleon-rs
text:
Already on Chameleon?
Put this at the very top of your app’s entry point, before anything imports Chameleon:
import chameleon_rs.compat

chameleon_rs.compat.install()
From then on import chameleon gives chameleon-rs, and so do chameleon_partials, chameleon_flask, fastapi_chameleon and chameleon_robyn. Templates and code stay as they are.

Same output. Chameleon’s own test suite passes unmodified, all 122 of its fixture templates render byte-identical, and so does every page of two production Flask/Quart sites. See Compatibility.
Check your own app first. Shadow mode renders a sample of real traffic with both engines and reports any difference, while Chameleon keeps serving. See Switching from Chameleon.

title: chameleon-rs
text:
Starting fresh?
Chameleon templates are HTML with tal: attributes and ${...} expressions, so a template is still valid HTML that an editor or browser opens as-is. Point chameleon-rs at a folder and decorate your views. With FastAPI:
import fastapi

import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.configure(template_folder='templates', app=app)


@app.get('/episodes/{number}')                      # the route decorator first...
@fastapi_chameleon.template('episodes/detail.pt')   # ...then @template
async def detail(number: int):
    episode = await db.episode(number)
    if episode is None:
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found()
    return {'episode': episode}
Getting started walks through it, and Web frameworks shows the same page in every framework.

title: chameleon-rs
text:
What’s new compared with Chameleon

Async rendering. await template.render_async(**model) awaits awaitable model values where the template uses them, without blocking the event loop. Opt-in settings run helpers and partials concurrently.
Web frameworks. Flask and Quart, FastAPI, Starlette (a drop-in for Jinja2Templates), Robyn and Litestar (a template engine for TemplateConfig) are built in; Pyramid’s pyramid_chameleon runs unchanged.
Partials. ${render_partial('shared/card.pt', item=item)} works in every template and renders natively, about 10x faster than Chameleon with chameleon_partials.
Markdown. ${markdown: post.body} converts CommonMark plus the GitHub extensions while the page renders, in Rust, with raw HTML escaped by default: about 26x faster than mistune, a pure-Python converter.
One place for settings. chameleon_rs.configure() sets the template folder, reloading, partial lookup and Markdown for the whole process.
Free-threaded Python. Wheels for 3.14t and 3.15t that keep the GIL off.
Typed. Type information for the whole API, checked with ty.

title: chameleon-rs
text:
Fast
Rendering is about 4x to 7x faster than Chameleon on synthetic pages, and 2.2x faster across the pages of a production site, where the app’s own Python code takes much of the time. Templates compile about 70x faster, so the first request after a deploy or reload is quick too. See Performance.

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Adapted from Chameleon’s language reference (source), modified for chameleon-rs. Used under Chameleon’s license; see LICENSE.txt and COPYRIGHT.txt in the repository.
The template attribute language is used to create dynamic XML-like content. It allows elements of a document to be replaced, repeated, or omitted.

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:attributes syntax:
argument             ::= attribute_statement [';' attribute_statement]*
attribute_statement  ::= (attribute_name expression | expression)
attribute_name       ::= [namespace-prefix ':'] Name
namespace-prefix     ::= Name

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The tal:attributes statement replaces the value of an attribute (or drops, or creates an attribute) with a dynamic value. The value of each expression is converted to a string, if necessary.






Note



You can qualify an attribute name with a namespace prefix, for example html:table, if you are generating an XML document with multiple namespaces.


If an attribute expression evaluates to None, the attribute is deleted from the statement element (or simply not inserted).
If an attribute statement is just an expression, it must evaluate to a Python dict (or implement the methods update() and items() from the dictionary specification).
If the expression evaluates to the symbol default (a symbol which is always available when evaluating attributes), its value is defined as the default static attribute value. If there is no such default value, a return value of default will drop the attribute.
If you use tal:attributes on an element with an active tal:replace command, the tal:attributes statement is ignored.
If you use tal:attributes on an element with a tal:repeat statement, the replacement is made on each repetition of the element, and the replacement expression is evaluated fresh for each repetition.






Note



If you want to include a semicolon (“;”) in an expression, it must be escaped by doubling it (“;;”). Similarly, you can escape expression interpolation using the “\(" symbol by doubling
it ("\)$”).

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Examples
Replacing a link:
<a href="/sample/link.html"
   tal:attributes="href context.url()"
   >
   ...
</a>
Replacing two attributes:
<textarea rows="80" cols="20"
          tal:attributes="rows request.rows();cols request.cols()"
    />
Inserting several attributes from a dict:
<a tal:attributes="{'href': '/x', 'class': 'c'}">x</a>
which renders as <a href="/x" class="c">x</a>.
A checkbox input:
<input type="checkbox" tal:attributes="checked True" />
checked is a boolean attribute: a true value renders it as checked="checked", and a false value drops it. In HTML templates the standard HTML boolean attributes (checked, selected, disabled and the rest) are treated this way by default. The boolean_attributes option replaces that set; XML templates have none unless you pass it:
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate, PageTemplateLoader

template = PageTemplate('<input type="checkbox" tal:attributes="checked True" />',
                        boolean_attributes={"selected", "checked"})
# or
templates = PageTemplateLoader(path, boolean_attributes={"selected", "checked"})

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:condition syntax:
argument ::= expression

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The tal:condition statement includes the statement element in the template only if the condition is met, and omits it otherwise. If its expression evaluates to a true value, then normal processing of the element continues, otherwise the statement element is immediately removed from the template. For these purposes, the value nothing is false.






Note



Like Python itself, ZPT considers None, zero, empty strings, empty sequences, empty dictionaries, and instances which return zero from __len__ or false from __bool__ to be false; all other values are true.








Note



default is defined only where a statement has a default to fall back on (tal:attributes, tal:content, tal:replace, tal:case). In tal:condition, tal:define and tal:repeat it raises NameError, in Chameleon as in chameleon-rs.

title: Basics (TAL)
Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:content syntax:
argument ::= (['text'] | 'structure') expression

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
Rather than replacing an entire element, you can insert text or structure in place of its children with the tal:content statement. The statement argument is exactly like that of tal:replace, and is interpreted in the same fashion. If the expression evaluates to nothing (or None), the statement element is left childless. If the expression evaluates to default, then the element’s contents are evaluated.
The default replacement behavior is text, which replaces angle-brackets and ampersands with their HTML entity equivalents. The structure keyword passes the replacement text through unchanged, allowing HTML/XML markup to be inserted. This can break your page if the text contains unanticipated markup (eg. text submitted via a web form), which is the reason that it is not the default.






Note



The structure keyword exists to provide backwards compatibility. In Chameleon, the structure: expression type provides the same functionality (also for inline expressions).

title: Basics (TAL)
Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:define syntax:
variable_name  ::= Name | '(' Name [',' Name]* ')'
define_var     ::= variable_name expression
define_scope   ::= (['local'] | 'global') define_var
argument       ::= define_scope [';' define_scope]*

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The tal:define statement defines variables. When you define a local variable in a statement element, you can use that variable in that element and the elements it contains. If you redefine a variable in a contained element, the new definition hides the outer element’s definition within the inner element.
Note that valid variable names are any Python identifier string including underscore, although two or more leading underscores are disallowed (used internally by the compiler). Further, names are case-sensitive.
Variable names support basic iterable unpacking when surrounded by parenthesis. This also applies to the variable established by tal:repeat.






Note



This is a Chameleon-specific language extension.


Python builtins are always “in scope”, and may be redefined (such as help or len).
The names econtext and rcontext are reserved: defining them is a compile error. Defining translate or decode has no effect (the template’s own translation function and decoder are used).
If the expression associated with a variable evaluates to nothing, then that variable has the value nothing, and may be used as such in further expressions.
You can define two different kinds of variables: local and global. When you define a local variable in a statement element, you can only use that variable in that element and the elements it contains. If you redefine a local variable in a contained element, the new definition hides the outer element’s definition within the inner element. When you define a global variable, you can use it in any element processed after the defining element. If you redefine a global variable, you replace its definition for the rest of the template.






Tip



Global variables may be changed by the execution of a macro if that macro also declares the variable to be global.


To set the definition scope of a variable, use the keywords local or global in front of the assignment. The default setting is local; thus, in practice, only the global keyword is used.






Note



If you want to include a semicolon (“;”) in an expression, it must be escaped by doubling it (“;;”).

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Examples
Defining a variable:
tal:define="company_name 'Zope Corp, Inc.'"
Defining two variables, where the second depends on the first:
tal:define="mytitle context.title; tlen len(mytitle)"
Defining a local and global variable:
tal:define="global mytitle context.title; tlen len(mytitle)"
Unpacking a sequence:
tal:define="(key,value) ('a', 42)"

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:case and tal:switch syntax:
argument ::= expression

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The switch and case construct is a short-hand syntax for matching a set of expressions against a single parent.
The tal:switch statement is used to set a new parent expression and the contained tal:case statements are then matched in sequence such that only the first match succeeds.
Note that the symbol default affirms the case precisely when no previous case has been successful. It should therefore be placed last.






Note



These statements are only available in Chameleon (2.x and later) and are not part of the ZPT specification.

title: Basics (TAL)
Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:omit-tag syntax:
argument ::= [ expression ]

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The tal:omit-tag statement leaves the contents of an element in place while omitting the surrounding start and end tags.
If the expression evaluates to a false value, then normal processing of the element continues and the tags are not omitted. If the expression evaluates to a true value, or no expression is provided, the statement element is replaced with its contents.






Note



Like Python itself, ZPT considers None, zero, empty strings, empty sequences, empty dictionaries, and instances which return zero from __len__ or false from __bool__ to be false; all other values are true.

title: Basics (TAL)
Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:repeat syntax:
argument      ::= variable_name expression
variable_name ::= Name

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The tal:repeat statement replicates a sub-tree of your document once for each item in a sequence. The expression should evaluate to a sequence. If the sequence is empty, then the statement element is deleted, otherwise it is repeated for each value in the sequence.
The variable_name is used to define a local variable and a repeat variable. For each repetition, the local variable is set to the current sequence element, and the repeat variable is set to an iteration object.

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Repeat variables
You use repeat variables to access information about the current repetition (such as the repeat index). The repeat variable has the same name as the local variable, but is only accessible through the built-in variable named repeat.
The following information is available from the repeat variable:







Attribute
Description




index
Repetition number, starting from zero.


number
Repetition number, starting from one.


even
True for even-indexed repetitions (0, 2, 4, …).


odd
True for odd-indexed repetitions (1, 3, 5, …).


parity
For odd-indexed repetitions, this is ‘odd’, else ‘even’.


start
True for the starting repetition (index 0).


end
True for the ending, or final, repetition.


length
Length of the sequence, which will be the total number of repetitions.


letter
Repetition number as a lower-case letter: “a” - “z”, then “ba” - “bz”, “ca” - “cz”, …, “zz”, “baa”, and so forth (the index written in base 26, with “a” as zero).


Letter
Upper-case version of letter.


roman
Repetition number as a lower-case roman numeral: “i”, “ii”, “iii”, “iv”, “v”, etc.


Roman
Upper-case version of roman.



The true and false values are not booleans: even and odd are the strings 'even' and 'odd' when true and '' when false, and start and end are 1 or 0. They test the same way in a condition, but print differently.
You can access the contents of the repeat variable using either dictionary- or attribute-style access, e.g. repeat['item'].start or repeat.item.start.






Note



For legacy compatibility, the attributes odd, even, number, letter, Letter, roman, and Roman are callable (returning self).








Note



Earlier versions of this document, and the Zope Page Templates Reference, referred to first and last attributes for use with sorted sequences. These are not implemented in Chameleon or the Zope reference implementation zope.tales. Instead, you can use itertools.groupby, as in the example below.

title: Basics (TAL)
Basics (TAL)
text:
Syntax
tal:replace syntax:
argument ::= ['structure'] expression

title: Basics (TAL)
text:
Description
The tal:replace statement replaces an element with dynamic content. It replaces the statement element with either text or a structure (unescaped markup). The body of the statement is an expression with an optional type prefix. The value of the expression is converted into an escaped string unless you provide the ‘structure’ prefix. Escaping consists of converting & to &, < to <, and > to >.






Note



If the inserted object provides an __html__ method, that method is called with the result inserted as structure. This feature is not implemented by ZPT.


If the expression evaluates to None, the element is simply removed. If the value is default, then the element is left unchanged.

title: Basics (TAL)
Extensions and differences
text: Adapted from Chameleon’s language reference (source), modified for chameleon-rs. Used under Chameleon’s license; see LICENSE.txt and COPYRIGHT.txt in the repository.

title: Extensions and differences
Extensions and differences
text:
Tuple unpacking
The tal:define and tal:repeat statements support tuple unpacking:
tal:define="(a, b, c) [1, 2, 3]"
Extended iterable unpacking using the asterisk character is not currently supported (even for versions of Python that support it natively).

title: Extensions and differences
section: Dictionary lookup as fallback after attribute error

title: Extensions and differences
Extensions and differences
Extensions and differences
text:
Literal content
While the tal:content and tal:replace attributes both support the structure keyword which inserts the content as a literal (without XML-escape), an object may also provide an __html__ method to the same effect.
The result of the method will be inserted as structure.

title: Extensions and differences
text:
Switch statement
Two new attributes have been added: tal:switch and tal:case. A case attribute works like a condition and only allows content if the value matches that of the nearest parent switch value.

title: Extensions and differences
Extensions and differences
Extensions and differences
text:
Default expression
The default expression type is Python.

title: Extensions and differences
Extensions and differences
text:
Special symbols
The CONTEXTS symbol is not available.
The z3c.pt package works as a compatibility layer for Chameleon. The template classes in this package provide an implementation which is fully compatible with ZPT.

title: Inline syntax
Robyn
text:
chameleon_rs.robyn renders templates from Robyn route handlers. It has chameleon-robyn’s API, so moving an app over is an import change, or no change at all with chameleon_rs.compat.install() (which makes import chameleon_robyn give this module).
import chameleon_rs doesn’t import Robyn. Only import chameleon_rs.robyn does. There is nothing extra to install: it uses the Robyn your app already has.






NotePython versions



Robyn publishes wheels for CPython 3.10 to 3.14 only (no 3.15 and no free-threaded build yet), so chameleon_rs.robyn works wherever Robyn installs. The examples on this page are not run when the docs are built, as the other framework pages are.



A first handler
from robyn import Robyn

import chameleon_rs.robyn as chameleon_robyn

app = Robyn(__file__)
chameleon_robyn.configure(template_folder='templates', auto_reload=dev_mode, app=app)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_robyn.template('home/index.pt')
async def index(query_params):
    videos = ['intro', 'partials', 'async']
    return {'message': 'Hello', 'videos': videos[: int(query_params.get('limit', '2'))]}


app.start(port=8080)
The handler returns the template’s model, and @template renders it into a robyn.Response with Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8. The decorated handler keeps its signature, so Robyn passes it the same request parts (request, query_params, path parameters, …) as without @template.
configure() here is the same call as chameleon_rs.configure(), so it also tells render_partial where templates live. app= turns on the decorator-order check below. global_init(template_folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True, restricted_namespace=True) is chameleon-robyn’s call and still works.


Decorator order
@template goes below the route decorator. Written above it, Robyn registers the bare handler, the template never renders and the route quietly returns the handler’s dict as JSON. An app given to configure(..., app=app) checks this when it starts:
@chameleon_robyn.template('home/about.pt')   # wrong: above the route
@app.get('/about')
def about():
    return {'message': 'About'}


app.start(port=8080)
# chameleon_rs.web.DecoratorOrderError: @template must be placed below the route decorator
# (@app.get, @app.post, @router.get, app.add_route, ...) on about() at app.py:12
# (route GET /about): the route was registered with the undecorated view, so its template
# never renders. Put the route decorator first (outermost) and @template under it.
The check runs in app.start(), in the main process before the server starts, so a misordered app fails to start. Robyn’s own startup hook was not used: an app has one startup handler (a second startup_handler replaces the first) and Robyn runs it inside each server process. Robyn’s in-process test client (robyn.testing.TestClient(app)) never calls start(), so the check also runs whenever the app’s route table is read with routes added since the last check, which the test client does when it is built: a misordered app fails there too. Reading the table early (a route listing built at import time) does not end the check: routes added afterwards are checked at the next read and in start(). Once start() passed the check, both hooks remove themselves.
Routes of a SubRouter included with app.include_router(...) are checked with the app. chameleon_robyn.check_views(app) (or a SubRouter) runs the same check on demand. A function registered raw on purpose (JSON on one route) and also decorated on another route is not flagged. One pattern can’t be told from the mistake: a function routed raw on this app whose @template wrapper is used somewhere else (called from another handler, or routed on another app). For such an app, pass check_order=False to configure() and keep the check in a test with chameleon_robyn.check_views(app, ignore=[that_function]).


Sync and async handlers

An async def handler renders its page with render_async on Robyn’s event loop. A model value that is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future) is awaited where the template uses it, so a slow query can be handed to the template unawaited, and other requests keep being served while it waits.
A plain def handler renders with render() where Robyn runs it: on its Rust worker thread, not on the event loop and not in a thread pool. While it renders, that worker (one per process by default) handles nothing else, as with chameleon-robyn.

@template(..., concurrent=True) renders render_partial(...) calls with awaitable arguments concurrently; @template(..., offload=True) (experimental) renders in a worker thread. Both apply to async def handlers only.


What a handler can return

A model: a dict, any other mapping, a dataclass instance (its fields, shallowly) or a Pydantic model (anything with a callable model_dump()).
A response: a robyn.Response passes through unchanged (redirects, custom errors).

Anything else raises chameleon_rs.robyn.ChameleonRobynException.
A __response_callback__ in the model is not a template variable: it is called with the response before it is returned, to set cookies or headers. The handler’s dict is not changed, so a shared or module-level model keeps working.
def remember(response):
    response.set_cookie('session', session_id)

@app.post('/login')
@chameleon_robyn.template('account/welcome.pt')
def login(request):
    return {'user': user, '__response_callback__': remember}


The @template decorator
@chameleon_robyn.template('home/index.pt')                       # a template path
@chameleon_robyn.template('feed.pt', 'application/xml')          # content_type=, or mimetype=
@chameleon_robyn.template('home/created.pt', status_code=201)
@chameleon_robyn.template                                        # no arguments
With no path, it renders {module}/{function}.html, where {module} is the last part of the handler’s module name; if there’s no .html file in the template folder, it uses {module}/{function}.pt. As in chameleon-robyn, the choice is made at the first request, once a template folder is configured, so handlers can be decorated at import time and global_init() called later from main().


Error pages
Inside a decorated handler, not_found() and error() stop the handler and render an error page as text/html. The template gets message ('The URL resulted in a 404 response.' or 'The URL resulted in an error.') and the data passed:
@app.get('/videos/:name')
@chameleon_robyn.template('home/index.pt')
async def video(name):
    if name not in videos:
        chameleon_robyn.not_found(name=name)   # renders errors/404.pt with status 404
    return {'message': name, 'videos': [name]}

not_found(template_file='errors/404.pt', **data) renders the page with status 404 (four04template_file= is chameleon-robyn’s name for the template).
error(template_file, status_code=500, **data) renders any error page.
generic_error(template_file, status_code, template_data) is fastapi-chameleon’s name and signature for error().







WarningTemplate names come from your code



The names given to @template, render(), response(), not_found() / error(), ChameleonTemplate.render_template() and render_partial() are looked up as the original libraries look them up, which allows .. and absolute paths. Write them in your code; never build one from a request (a path or query parameter, a header).




Rendering without the decorator
html = chameleon_robyn.render('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)        # a str
html = await chameleon_robyn.render_async('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)
resp = chameleon_robyn.response('feed.pt', 'application/xml', items=items)
resp = await chameleon_robyn.response_async('feed.pt', status_code=201, items=items)
Both raise ChameleonRobynException if nothing has been configured.


Robyn’s template interface
ChameleonTemplate implements Robyn’s TemplateInterface, as its JinjaTemplate does. It has a loader of its own and needs no configure():
from chameleon_rs.robyn import ChameleonTemplate

templates = ChameleonTemplate('templates', auto_reload=dev_mode)


@app.get('/about')
async def about():
    return await templates.render_template_async('home/about.pt', message='About')
render_template(name, **data) returns a 200 robyn.Response; render_template_async is its coroutine. robyn.templating.render(name, template_engine=ChameleonTemplate, ...) works too, and type-checks there. (At runtime ChameleonTemplate follows Robyn’s interface without subclassing its abstract class, which would import Jinja2, as chameleon-robyn does.)


Coming from chameleon-robyn







chameleon-robyn
chameleon-rs




global_init(folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True, restricted_namespace=True)
Still works, and takes app=. It configures the handlers only, as before, and ignores a second call. configure() sets handlers and partials together, and every call applies.


@template(file, content_type, status_code), render, response, not_found, clear, ChameleonTemplate
Same. @template also takes mimetype=, concurrent= and offload=; not_found also takes template_file= and template data.


—
error(), generic_error(), render_async(), response_async(), ChameleonTemplate.render_template_async(), check_views().


ChameleonRobynException, ChameleonRobynNotFoundException
Same names, now subclasses of chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError and NotFound.


Handlers return a dict
Also mappings, dataclasses and Pydantic models.


Async handlers render synchronously
They render with render_async; an awaitable model value is awaited where the template uses it.



Settings are process-wide: a Robyn handler has no app to find settings of its own in.

title: Compatibility
text: chameleon-rs’s goal is to produce exactly what Chameleon produces, for every template, and to raise the same errors. This page says how that’s measured, and lists the few places where chameleon-rs knowingly differs.

title: Compatibility
text:
Code blocks
Chameleon compiles <?python ... ?> blocks into the template’s render function, so what a block defines is a local of that call. chameleon-rs runs a block in a namespace kept per template and render, which differs in two ways:

Recursive partials share it. Two frames of the same template in one render (a partial that renders itself) see each other’s block definitions, where each Chameleon call has its own.
default and attrs inside a block are ordinary names. Chameleon aliases them there as in expressions (the default marker and the element’s attributes).

title: Compatibility
text:
render_partial in econtext
With chameleon_partials, render_partial is a model value, so it shows up in the template’s econtext and in the argument list of a render error. The built-in render_partial is a builtin of every template, so it is not in either.

title: Compatibility
text:
Corner cases in slot bodies
Three cases, all involving the slot fills of a macro call together with tal:on-error or i18n settings, render differently. No real template we’ve seen does this; each is pinned by a test that fails if the behaviour changes.

A failing expression under a handler in a slot body whose slot sits inside i18n:translate or i18n:name. Chameleon writes a text node and its expressions as one piece, so when an expression fails, the text before it in the same node is dropped with it. chameleon-rs writes that text first, so it stays (<q>Q where Chameleon gives <q>).
A handler on an i18n:name element whose content calls a macro that fails partway: the same difference, for the text of the failing node inside the macro.
A fill no macro took, used by a later macro call while the calling template has different i18n:domain, i18n:context or i18n:target settings: values converted by that fill use the settings where it was defined. Chameleon uses the settings at the later call.

title: Compatibility
text:
Behaviour of the helper libraries
The built-ins differ from chameleon_partials, chameleon-flask, fastapi-chameleon and chameleon-robyn in a few ways that don’t affect templates that worked before:

Partial paths. A path that isn’t in the configured template folder is also looked for next to the calling template, where chameleon_partials would raise. configure(partial_search='registered') restores the original lookup. See Partials.
Async views await model values. An async view renders with render_async, so a model value that is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future, or a test double such as AsyncMock()) is awaited where the template uses it. The original libraries rendered the object itself.
Setup. Every configure() call applies (register_extensions ignored later calls), and configure(..., app=app) checks the decorator order at startup.

title: Compatibility
text:
render_async and a replaced render
render_async() honours a render() that a subclass overrides, since the override may add defaults or post-process the output: it calls it, synchronously, so awaitable values are not awaited. Assigning a new function to PageTemplate.render (a monkeypatch, for example to time renders) counts as such an override. Every render_async(), including the async views of the framework integrations, then renders synchronously through your function. See Migrating for a way to time both.

title: Performance
text:
chameleon-rs compiles a template to a native program and runs it in Rust. The template’s own work (the loops, conditions, escaping, macro and slot calls, partials and output assembly) happens without Python bytecode. Python only runs where the template calls into your code: an attribute lookup, a method call, a helper.
