This matters after every deploy, every worker restart and every auto_reload change.


Real applications
On real pages, the template engine is only part of the work. In a production Quart site, measured page by page with both engines on the same data:

Template rendering was 2.2x faster in total, with a median of 2.9x per page.
Whole requests, including the app’s database and Python code, were 1.3x faster.
Under load, with 20 concurrent users on one single-threaded worker, throughput rose 34%, median latency fell from 170 ms to 120 ms, and p99 latency fell from 255 ms to 195 ms.

The HTML was identical on every page. In chameleon-rs’s renders there, the engine’s own code was only 3–6% of the time. The rest was CPython work the templates trigger: attribute lookups, small helpers and properties, and conversions.


Getting the most out of it

Keep templates loaded. Reuse PageTemplateLoader instances and template objects. Building a template per request recompiles it every time.
Leave auto_reload off in production. It checks the file’s modification time on every render.
Write partials as a whole expression: ${render_partial('card.pt', item=item)}. Then the partial renders natively, without a Python call.
Prepare data in the view. Expensive properties and helpers called inside a loop cost the same on either engine.



Reproduce the numbers
The benchmarks are in the repository’s bench/ folder. Build a release first:
make dev             # one-time setup: venv, reference Chameleon, extension
make build-release
venv/bin/python bench/bench_ab.py <git-ref> --scenario listing   # also: macro, page
venv/bin/python bench/bench_page.py
venv/bin/python bench/bench_skeleton.py
venv/bin/python bench/bench_macros.py
venv/bin/python bench/bench_first.py
Each script prints chameleon-rs’s and Chameleon’s times from the same run. Run them on a quiet machine. Background load moves the absolute numbers much more than the ratios.

title: Pyramid
text:
Chameleon grew up with Pyramid, and pyramid_chameleon is how most Pyramid apps render .pt templates. chameleon-rs has no Pyramid module of its own because it doesn’t need one: pyramid_chameleon runs unchanged on chameleon-rs through chameleon_rs.compat.install(). Your views, renderer= names, templates and settings stay as they are.






NoteNot run when the docs are built



The examples on this page are checked by hand against Pyramid 2.1 and pyramid_chameleon 0.3, not run when the docs are built, as the other framework pages are.



Switch an app over
Install chameleon-rs next to Pyramid and pyramid_chameleon:
uv pip install chameleon-rs pyramid pyramid_chameleon
pyramid_chameleon depends on stock Chameleon, so pip installs that too. That’s fine: once the alias is installed, nothing imports it.
Then install the alias where your app starts. With pserve, that’s the top of the package whose main() your .ini file names (use = egg:myapp), above every other import:
# myapp/__init__.py
import chameleon_rs.compat

chameleon_rs.compat.install()

from pyramid.config import Configurator


def main(global_config, **settings):
    with Configurator(settings=settings) as config:
        config.include('pyramid_chameleon')
        config.add_route('home', '/')
        config.scan('.views')
    return config.make_wsgi_app()
config.include('pyramid_chameleon') imports pyramid_chameleon, which imports chameleon, and gets chameleon-rs. Every .pt (and .txt) renderer in the app now renders on chameleon-rs.
Other entry points need the same two lines first: a conftest.py for your tests, and any script that loads the app without pserve (pshell and prequest go through main(), so they’re covered).


Views and templates
Nothing changes in a view:
# myapp/views.py
from pyramid.view import view_config


@view_config(route_name='home', renderer='templates/home.pt')
def home(request):
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': ['intro', 'partials']}
Or in its template:
<!-- myapp/templates/home.pt -->
<html metal:use-macro="load: layout.pt">
  <main metal:fill-slot="content">
    <h1>${title}</h1>
    <div tal:repeat="video videos">${render_partial('shared/video.pt', video=video)}</div>
    <p>${request.path}</p>
  </main>
</html>
What pyramid_chameleon provides keeps working:

Renderer names: relative names (templates/home.pt), asset specs (myapp:templates/home.pt) and absolute paths.
Macro renderers: renderer='templates/fragments#count.pt' renders only the count macro of fragments.pt, handy for HTMX fragments.
Text templates: .txt renderers use PageTextTemplateFile.
The system values: request, context, view and renderer_name in every template.
Settings: pyramid.reload_templates turns on auto_reload, and debug_templates works as before.
Translation: pyramid_chameleon’s translator, so i18n:translate uses Pyramid’s localizer.
pyramid.renderers.render() and render_to_response() with a .pt name.



Partials
render_partial is built into every template. A partial path is looked for next to the calling template and in the folders above it, up to your package’s templates folder, so shared/video.pt above is found with no setup. Nothing outside that folder is searched.
To render partials from Python as well (an HTMX view returning one fragment, say), tell chameleon-rs where the templates live once, in main():
from pathlib import Path

import chameleon_rs

chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=(Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix())
Then chameleon_rs.render_partial('shared/video.pt', video=v).html_text returns the markup.
If your app added render_partial with chameleon_partials and a BeforeRender subscriber, the subscriber can go. With the alias it still works, and calls the built-in. See Partials and Migrating.


Rendering is synchronous
Pyramid is a WSGI framework: views and renderers run synchronously, in your server’s worker threads. pyramid_chameleon calls the template’s render(), so the async features (Async rendering) don’t apply. You still get the speed: rendering is several times faster, and templates compile about 70x faster, so the first request after a restart or a template change is quick too.


Precompiling isn’t needed
pyramid_chameleon’s pyramid-chameleon-precompile script fills CHAMELEON_CACHE with compiled Python modules, to save compile time at startup. chameleon-rs doesn’t write a cache (see Compatibility), and compiling 100 templates takes about 10 ms, so drop the script from your deployment. If you keep it, its worker processes need the alias too: they import chameleon without running your app’s main().


Compatibility
pyramid_chameleon’s own test suite passes on chameleon-rs, unmodified: it runs in chameleon-rs’s integration tests on every change, together with the suites of the other framework libraries. See Compatibility.

title: Security
text:
Templates are code: like Python source, they run with your application’s rights, and an expression in one can do anything Python can. The data you render them with is what may come from users. This page says what chameleon-rs does with that data, where its protection stops, and what to do there. Everything here behaves exactly as in Chameleon unless it says otherwise.

What’s escaped

Text: ${x}, tal:content="x" and tal:replace="x" escape &, < and >.
Attribute values: title="${x}" and tal:attributes="title x" also escape the attribute’s own quote character (" as ", ' as ').
markdown:: in element content, raw HTML in the text is escaped and javascript:, vbscript:, file: and data: links are removed, unless a profile sets raw_html='allow'. In an attribute value the result is escaped like any string. See Markdown.

Nothing is escaped for structure, structure:, or an object with an __html__ method (such as Markup). Use them only for markup you made or have already sanitized.


Where escaping isn’t enough
These are the HTML contexts where escaping &, <, > and the quote doesn’t make data safe.

Attribute names from data. tal:attributes="attrs" with a dictionary escapes the values but writes the keys as they are. A key such as onclick="x" a adds an attribute. Build attribute dictionaries from fixed names only.
Unquoted attributes. In <p title=${x}>, a space in the value starts a new attribute (a onmouseover=alert(1)). Always quote attribute values.
CDATA sections. <![CDATA[${x}]]> is written unescaped. Keep data out of CDATA.
Inside <script> and <style>. ${x} there is HTML-escaped, which stops a </script> but not a quote: var name = "${x}"; can be broken out of. Put the data in an attribute instead and read it from JavaScript:
<div id="app" data-user="${user_json}"></div>
where user_json is json.dumps(...) of what the script needs.
URLs. href="${url}" is escaped, but a javascript: URL is still a script. Check the scheme of any URL that comes from users before you render it.
Translations. The text a translation function returns is written as markup, as in Chameleon. Treat message catalogs like templates: only from sources you trust.



Template names from requests
A name that comes from a request must never reach a lookup that accepts any path.

Safe with request data: render_partial, chameleon_rs.starlette.Templates, chameleon_rs.litestar.ChameleonEngine and chameleon_rs.robyn.ChameleonTemplate. They refuse names that leave their folder: absolute paths, .. out of it, package:path specs, backslashes on the Jinja-style APIs. A refused name is “not found”, like a missing file.
Names from code only: the decorator APIs (@template, render, response in each integration), PageTemplateLoader and load: expressions. They accept ../ and absolute paths, as the original libraries and Chameleon do.

If a page is chosen by the request, map the request value to a name you wrote:
PAGES = {'about': 'pages/about.pt', 'team': 'pages/team.pt'}
template = PAGES.get(slug)  # None for anything else: a 404


Render data
Keyword arguments to render() become names in the template, and they win over most built-in names: len, str and other Python builtins in expressions, and translate, target_language and nothing. (In <?python ?> code blocks, builtins can’t be replaced.) So never pass a request’s parameters straight in, as in render(**request.args). Build the data in your view, with the names the template expects.


Errors and logs
When a render fails, the error message lists the template’s variables and their values, as in Chameleon: strings appear as they are. That text goes to your logs. None of the framework integrations put it in an HTTP response: you get the framework’s own error page, unless its debug mode is on. Keep debug mode off in production, and don’t render with secrets that the template doesn’t need.
Shadow mode logs up to 4 KB of the difference between the two engines’ output, which can include users’ data. It’s meant for staging, and it’s off unless you install it.


Untrusted input size
chameleon-rs keeps the cost of a render in proportion to its input:

Wide Markdown tables convert in linear time.
The Markdown cache has a limit in entries and in bytes.
A template nested too deeply to compile raises RecursionError instead of crashing the process.

A large input still costs time in proportion to its size, so limit the size of what users can submit (a comment’s length, say) in your application, as you would anyway.

title: Litestar
text:
chameleon_rs.litestar renders templates from Litestar route handlers, two ways:
import chameleon_rs doesn’t import Litestar. Only import chameleon_rs.litestar does, and it uses the Litestar your app already has (2.x; tested with 2.25).

title: Litestar
text:
.pt and the media type
Litestar picks a Template response’s media type from the template name’s suffix, and Python’s mimetypes doesn’t know .pt: with litestar.response.Template, a .pt page is served as text/plain, and the browser shows its source. chameleon_rs.litestar.Template is a subclass that serves a name Litestar can’t guess as text/html:

from litestar.response import Template as LitestarTemplate


@get('/stock')
async def stock() -> LitestarTemplate:
    return LitestarTemplate('home/index.pt', context={'title': 'Stock', 'videos': []})


app = Litestar(
    [index, stock, video],
    template_config=TemplateConfig(engine=ChameleonEngine, directory=template_folder),
)
with TestClient(app) as client:
    print('ours: ', client.get('/').headers['content-type'])
    print('stock:', client.get('/stock').headers['content-type'])

INFO - 2026-10-22 11:39:45,881 - httpx - _client - HTTP Request: GET http://testserver.local/ "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"
INFO - 2026-10-22 11:39:45,882 - httpx - _client - HTTP Request: GET http://testserver.local/stock "HTTP/1.1 200 OK"


ours:  text/html; charset=utf-8
stock: text/plain; charset=utf-8


Names Litestar can guess keep their type (.html, .xml, .txt), and a media_type you give, on the Template or on the route (@get(..., media_type=...)), wins. Litestar’s HTMXTemplate and other Template subclasses need media_type='text/html' for .pt names. (Registering the type globally, mimetypes.add_type('text/html', '.pt') at startup, also works, for every library in the process.)
The response class matters, not only the template: a handler annotated -> Any or -> dict that returns a Template is served with Content-Type: application/json (the route’s media type wins; the same with stock Litestar): annotate it -> Template.

title: Litestar
text:
Synchronous rendering
Litestar’s template protocol is synchronous: its Template response calls the engine’s render() while it builds the response, on the event loop. ChameleonEngine can’t change that, so a Template response never awaits anything and a slow page blocks the loop while it renders. For an async def handler that should render without blocking, use the decorator API below, which renders with render_async.

title: Litestar
text:
The handler’s signature
Litestar builds dependency injection, validation and the OpenAPI schema from the handler’s signature and its return annotation. @template keeps the parameters (path and query parameters, FromPath/FromQuery, dependencies, data), with two changes Litestar reads:

The return annotation becomes litestar.Response. A handler annotated -> dict would otherwise be a JSON route: Litestar would pick application/json and could apply a return DTO.
A keyword-only request: Request parameter is added when the handler has none, so the template can get request and url_for. The wrapper takes it out before calling your handler; request is one of Litestar’s reserved names, so it is not in the OpenAPI schema.

Annotations are not evaluated when @template runs (a forward reference to a class defined later in the module resolves when Litestar registers the route). The OpenAPI schema describes the response as application/json, as for any handler returning Response; pass @get(..., media_type=MediaType.HTML) for an accurate schema.
Errors are chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError, NotFound, ErrorPage and DecoratorOrderError, also importable from chameleon_rs.litestar (a missing template here is Chameleon’s ValueError, as in the other integrations; ChameleonEngine raises Litestar’s TemplateNotFoundException).






WarningTemplate names come from your code



The names given to @template, render(), response(), not_found() / error() and render_partial() are looked up as the original libraries look them up, which allows .. and absolute paths. Write them in your code; never build one from a request (a path or query parameter, a header). ChameleonEngine refuses names that reach outside its folder, as Litestar’s Jinja engine does.

title: Migrating from the helper libraries
text:
chameleon-rs builds in what chameleon_partials, chameleon-flask, fastapi-chameleon and chameleon-robyn provide, and has its own Litestar engine. With chameleon_rs.compat.install() you don’t have to change anything: the old imports give the built-ins (see Switching from Chameleon for Chameleon itself). This page is for when you want to move to the new names, and drop the old setup code that’s no longer needed.

At a glance







Before
After




from chameleon import PageTemplateLoader
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateLoader


chameleon_partials.register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=dev) and chameleon_flask.global_init(folder, auto_reload=dev)
One call: chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=folder, auto_reload=dev)


return chameleon_partials.extend_model(model) in every view
return model: render_partial is in every template


A Pyramid BeforeRender subscriber that adds render_partial
Remove it


import chameleon_flask
import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask


import fastapi_chameleon
import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon


import chameleon_robyn
import chameleon_rs.robyn as chameleon_robyn


from litestar_chameleon import ChameleonTemplateEngine
from chameleon_rs.litestar import ChameleonEngine, and return chameleon_rs.litestar.Template


chameleon_partials.render_partial(path, **m).html_text
chameleon_rs.render_partial(path, **m).html_text


except chameleon_partials.PartialsException, except chameleon_flask.exceptions.FlaskChameleonException
Still work. except chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError catches both


has_registered_extensions = False in test teardown
chameleon_rs.partials.clear()





chameleon_partials
# Before
import chameleon_partials

chameleon_partials.register_extensions(template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)


def index(request):
    model = {'videos': videos}
    return chameleon_partials.extend_model(model)
# After
import chameleon_rs

chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)


def index(request):
    return {'videos': videos}
Templates don’t change. ${render_partial('shared/partials/video.pt', video=v)} works as before, and runs natively.
Things to know:

Every configure() call applies. register_extensions ignored a second call unless you passed cache_init=False. register_extensions itself still behaves the old way.
Partial paths can also be relative to the calling template. A path that isn’t in the template folder is looked for next to the calling template, where chameleon_partials would raise. Templates that worked before render exactly the same. configure(partial_search='registered') turns the extra lookup off.
Configuring is thread-safe. Configuration is swapped in whole, so a render never sees half of one.



chameleon-flask
# Before
import chameleon_flask

chameleon_flask.global_init(template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)
# After
import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)
Views, @template, render, response and not_found stay the same. New in chameleon-rs:

configure() also sets the partials folder, so you need only one setup call.
error(template_file, status_code=500, **data) renders any error page.
Views can return mappings, dataclasses and Pydantic models, not only dict.
configure(..., app=app) gives one app its own configuration.

See Flask and Quart.


fastapi-chameleon
import fastapi_chameleon
becomes
import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon
or stays as it is with chameleon_rs.compat.install(). Every name keeps working (global_init, @template, render, response, not_found, generic_error, clear, the exception classes), and its test suite passes unmodified on the built-in. Differences:

Async views render with render_async: an awaitable model value is awaited where the template uses it.
configure(..., app=app) (or global_init(..., app=app)) checks at startup that every @template sits below its route decorator.
error(), render_async(), response_async(), and status_code= on @template.

See FastAPI.


chameleon-robyn
import chameleon_robyn
becomes
import chameleon_rs.robyn as chameleon_robyn
or stays as it is with chameleon_rs.compat.install(). Every name keeps working (global_init, @template, render, response, not_found, clear, ChameleonTemplate, __response_callback__, the exception classes), and its test suite passes unmodified on the built-in. Differences:

Async handlers render with render_async: an awaitable model value is awaited where the template uses it.
configure(..., app=app) (or global_init(..., app=app)) checks in app.start() (and when Robyn’s test client is built) that every @template sits below its route decorator.
error(), render_async(), response_async(), data for not_found(), and ChameleonTemplate.render_template_async().

See Robyn.


litestar-chameleon
litestar-chameleon is a third-party package, not built in: it keeps working as it is with chameleon_rs.compat.install(). To move to the built-in engine instead:
from litestar_chameleon import ChameleonTemplateEngine
from litestar.response import Template
becomes
from chameleon_rs.litestar import ChameleonEngine as ChameleonTemplateEngine
from chameleon_rs.litestar import Template   # .pt served as text/html
Differences: url_for_static_asset is registered too, a name outside the template folder is refused, a context key wins over a template callable of the same name (as for Jinja), the loader options are ChameleonEngine arguments (CHAMELEON_RELOAD rather than CHAMELEON_AUTO_RELOAD), and stock Chameleon need not be installed. See Litestar.


Timing renders
Instrumentation that replaces PageTemplate.render to time every render (common in apps that log slow templates) changes how async renders run on chameleon-rs. render_async() honours a render() that differs from the built-in one, because a subclass’s override may add defaults or post-process the output, and a monkeypatched render looks exactly like that override. So with the patch in place, every render_async(), including those of async @template views, calls your render synchronously, and awaitable model values are not awaited.
# Makes every render_async() render synchronously:
original = PageTemplate.render

def timed_render(self, *args, **kwargs):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        return original(self, *args, **kwargs)
    finally:
        log_render(self.filename, time.perf_counter() - start)

PageTemplate.render = timed_render
Wrapping render_async as well doesn’t help: the original render_async still sees the replaced render. Instead:

Time the request or the view, in middleware or around the call that renders. The template’s share is then the view’s time minus its data loading.
Use a sampling profiler such as py-spy for a breakdown by template and helper, with no code change.
Keep the patch only in apps that render synchronously. There it changes nothing but the timing.

The same applies to a subclass that overrides render(): its render_async() renders synchronously through the override. See Compatibility.


Pitfalls

Install the alias first. chameleon_rs.compat.install() must run before the first import chameleon, including imports inside your framework integration. Put it in the entry point itself, above every other import.
A patched PageTemplate.render makes async renders synchronous. See Timing renders.
Don’t mix shadow mode with the alias. Shadow mode needs stock Chameleon as chameleon.
template.source isn’t Python. Code that read the generated module (rare, mostly debugging tools) gets a program dump instead. See Compatibility.

title: Template language
Configuration
text:
chameleon-rs has three layers of configuration:

chameleon_rs.configure(): process-wide settings for templates loaded by name, used by render_partial and the framework integrations.
Template options: keyword arguments to the template classes and PageTemplateLoader, exactly as in Chameleon.
Environment variables: Chameleon’s CHAMELEON_* variables.


chameleon_rs.configure()
import chameleon_rs

chameleon_rs.configure(
    template_folder='templates',
    auto_reload=False,
    restricted_namespace=True,
    partial_search='caller',
    markdown=True,
    markdown_cache=1024,
)



Option
Default
Meaning




template_folder
none, required on the first call
An existing directory. Partials and the framework integrations load templates by name from it.


auto_reload
False
Recompile a template when its file changes. For partials, each file is checked at most once per render. Use it in development only.


restricted_namespace
True
False allows attributes with other namespaces or prefixes, such as Alpine.js’s @click or Vue’s v-on:click.


partial_search
'caller'
Where render_partial looks: 'caller' searches the template folder, then the calling template’s search path and folders. 'registered' searches the template folder only, as chameleon_partials does. See Partials.


markdown
none
The markdown: expression: True for the defaults, or a dict of profiles (prefix → options). False removes it. See Markdown.


markdown_cache
1024
How many Markdown conversions to keep. 0 turns the cache off.



How it behaves:

An option you leave out keeps its current value. So configure(partial_search='registered') changes only the search mode.
Every call applies. There’s no cache_init as in chameleon_partials, chameleon-flask and fastapi-chameleon, so a second call with a different folder takes effect.
It’s safe with threads. Each configuration is an immutable object that’s swapped in whole, so a render running at the same time never sees half of one. Still, call it at startup, not per request.
partial_search and the Markdown settings don’t need a folder. Every other option needs one, on the first call.
It returns the new settings, and raises chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError for a missing folder, or ValueError for an unknown partial_search or an invalid Markdown setting (TypeError for one of the wrong type). A call that raises changes nothing.


import chameleon_rs

settings = chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=True)
print(settings.auto_reload, settings.restricted_namespace)

# Leaving options out keeps them: auto_reload is still True.
settings = chameleon_rs.configure(partial_search='registered')
print(settings.auto_reload)

True True
True


For tests, chameleon_rs.partials.clear(), chameleon_rs.flask.clear(), chameleon_rs.fastapi.clear(), chameleon_rs.starlette.clear(), chameleon_rs.robyn.clear() and chameleon_rs.litestar.clear() forget the configuration again. Starlette’s Templates() and Litestar’s ChameleonEngine() without a directory use this configuration too.
chameleon_rs.flask.configure(..., app=app) sets a configuration for one Flask or Quart app only. See Flask and Quart.


Template options
The template classes take Chameleon’s options as keyword arguments, or as class attributes on a subclass. PageTemplateLoader passes any extra keyword arguments on to each template it loads.
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateFile, PageTemplateLoader

page = PageTemplateFile('templates/home.pt', auto_reload=True, encoding='utf-8')
templates = PageTemplateLoader(['templates'], '.pt', restricted_namespace=False)
The common ones:








Option
Default
Meaning




auto_reload
False (or CHAMELEON_RELOAD)
File templates recompile when their file changes.


encoding
none
Lets you pass encoded byte strings as values.


translate
none
The translation function for i18n: attributes: translate(msgid, domain=None, mapping=None, default=None, context=None, target_language=None).


boolean_attributes
the HTML set, in HTML mode
Attributes rendered as name="name" for a true value and dropped for a false one.


strict
True
Compile every expression up front. False only requires an expression to be valid when it’s evaluated.


restricted_namespace
True
False passes unknown namespaces and prefixes through, for Alpine.js or Vue.


trim_attribute_space
False
Strip extra whitespace between attributes.


implicit_i18n_translate
False
Mark the text in every element for translation.


implicit_i18n_attributes
empty
Attribute names (lowercase) to mark for translation.


on_error_handler
none
Called with the exception in a tal:on-error fallback.


default_expression
'python'
The expression type used when there’s no prefix.


extra_builtins
empty
Extra names available in every template.


keep_body / keep_source
False
Keep the template’s source text, or a readable dump of its compiled program.



The rest are also accepted, as in Chameleon: default_marker, value_repr, tokenizer, debug, enable_data_attributes, enable_comment_interpolation and expression_types. File templates also take search_path, package_name, loader_class and prepend_relative_search_path.






Notesource is a program dump, not Python



Chameleon compiles a template to a Python module, and template.source is that module’s code. chameleon-rs compiles to a native program instead, so with keep_source=True, source holds a readable dump of the program. Nothing in Chameleon’s own tests depends on it being Python.




Environment variables
These are read once, when chameleon-rs is imported, as Chameleon reads them. The values y, yes, t, true, on and 1 (any case) count as true.







Variable
Effect




CHAMELEON_RELOAD
The default for auto_reload: file templates reload when their file changes.


CHAMELEON_EAGER
File templates compile when they’re created, not on first use. Handy in a test that checks every template in a project compiles.


CHAMELEON_DEBUG
Templates keep their body and a dump of their compiled program, and use a module loader in a temporary directory.


CHAMELEON_CACHE
A directory, which must exist. Chameleon writes the generated Python modules there. chameleon-rs checks the directory but doesn’t write compiled programs to disk: compiling is fast enough not to need it.



Unknown CHAMELEON_* variables are logged as warnings, as in Chameleon.

title: Async rendering
text:
Chameleon renders synchronously. In an async web app (FastAPI, Starlette, Quart, Litestar, Robyn) that means a render runs on the event loop, and nothing else in that worker runs until it finishes. chameleon-rs keeps render() exactly as it was and adds render_async(), which renders on the event loop without holding it while it waits for data.
The framework integrations use it for you: an async def view decorated with @template renders with render_async. This page explains what that does, and the opt-in extras built on it.

title: Async rendering
Async rendering
text:
Partials in parallel: concurrent=True
A template created with concurrent=True also renders its render_partial(...) calls concurrently, when a call has an awaitable argument. Each such partial renders as a render of its own, in a task:

import pathlib, tempfile

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(folder / 'card.pt').write_text('<div class="card">${data}</div>')
chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=str(folder))


async def load(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return name


page = PageTemplate("""\
<section tal:repeat="name names">${render_partial('card.pt', data=load(name))}</section>
""", concurrent=True)

start = time.perf_counter()
print(await page.render_async(names=['a', 'b', 'c'], load=load))
print(f'{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s')

<section><div class="card">a</div></section>
<section><div class="card">b</div></section>
<section><div class="card">c</div></section>

0.2s


The integrations take the same setting on the decorator: @template('page.pt', concurrent=True), and TemplateResponse_async(..., concurrent=True) for Starlette’s Templates.

title: Web frameworks
text:
chameleon-rs works with the Python web frameworks you’re likely to use, with nothing extra to install. Each integration is a module of chameleon-rs that imports its framework only when you import it, and uses the version your app already has.
Already using one of the libraries in the third column? chameleon_rs.compat.install() makes its import give the built-in, so the app runs unchanged. See Switching from Chameleon.

title: Web frameworks
text:
Async views
An async def view renders with render_async: a model value that is awaitable is awaited where the template uses it, and the render doesn’t block the event loop while it waits. A plain def view renders with render(), where the framework runs it. See Async rendering for the details and the opt-in concurrency settings.

title: Web frameworks
text:
What a template gets







Integration
Besides the model




Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Robyn
Nothing: the template gets what the view returns, as with the original libraries. Return request in the model if the template needs it.


Starlette
request and url_for, as with Jinja2Templates, plus its context processors with Templates.


Litestar
request, csrf_input, url_for, csrf_token, url_for_static_asset and your registered template callables.


Pyramid
request, context, view and renderer_name.



Every template also has render_partial built in, and markdown: once it’s turned on.

title: Web frameworks
Markdown
text:
chameleon-rs can convert Markdown to HTML while it renders, with a markdown: expression:
It’s opt-in: Chameleon has nothing like it, so you turn it on with configure() and use it in new templates. The converter is built into chameleon-rs (comrak, in Rust), so there’s no Markdown package to install.

title: Markdown
Flask and Quart
text:
chameleon_rs.flask renders templates from Flask and Quart views. It has chameleon-flask’s API, so moving an app over is an import change, or no change at all with chameleon_rs.compat.install().
import chameleon_rs doesn’t import Flask. Only import chameleon_rs.flask does.

A first view

import flask

import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
def index():
    return {'message': 'Hello', 'videos': ['intro', 'partials']}

The view returns the template’s model, and @template renders it into a flask.Response:

client = app.test_client()
print(client.get('/').text)

<h1>Hello</h1>
<ul><li><a href="/videos/intro">intro</a></li>
<li><a href="/videos/partials">partials</a></li></ul>


configure() here is the same call as chameleon_rs.configure(), so it also tells render_partial where templates live.


Decorator order
@template goes below the route decorator. Written above it, Flask registers the bare view, the template never renders and the route quietly returns the view’s dict as JSON. Give the app to configure() and it checks before its first request (Quart: when it starts serving):
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=template_folder, app=app)


@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')   # wrong: above the route
@app.get('/about')
def about():
    return {'message': 'About', 'videos': []}

# The first request raises chameleon_rs.web.DecoratorOrderError:
# @template must be placed below the route decorator (@app.route, @app.get,
# @blueprint.route, ...) on about() at app.py:12 (route GET /about): ...
Flask has no startup hook, so the check runs on the first request. Blueprints are included. chameleon_flask.check_views(app) runs the same check on demand, for example in a test. Once the check passes, the app runs without it.
One pattern can’t be told from the mistake: a function routed raw on this app whose @template wrapper is used somewhere else (called from another view, or routed on another app). For such an app, pass check_order=False to configure() and keep the check in a test with chameleon_flask.check_views(app, ignore=[that_function]).


What a view can return

A model: a dict, any other mapping, a dataclass instance (its fields, shallowly) or a Pydantic model (anything with a callable model_dump()).
A response: a flask.Response, a Quart response or a werkzeug response passes through unchanged. Use it for redirects.

Anything else raises chameleon_rs.flask.FlaskChameleonException.


The @template decorator
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')                            # a template path
@chameleon_flask.template('feed.pt', content_type='application/xml')  # or mimetype=
@chameleon_flask.template('home/created.pt', status_code=201)
@chameleon_flask.template                                             # no arguments
A text type without a charset gets ; charset=utf-8 (the default is text/html; charset=utf-8), as Flask’s own render_template responses do. chameleon-flask sent the bare type.
With no path, it renders {module}/{function}.html, where {module} is the last part of the view’s module name. If there’s no .html file in the template folder, it uses {module}/{function}.pt. It checks once, when the view is decorated.
It works on sync views, Flask’s async views and Quart views alike.


Error pages
Inside a decorated view, not_found() and error() stop the view and render an error page:

app = flask.Flask(__name__)


@app.get('/videos/<name>')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
def video(name):
    if name != 'intro':
        chameleon_flask.not_found(path=flask.request.path)   # renders errors/404.pt
    return {'message': name, 'videos': [name]}


response = app.test_client().get('/videos/missing')
print(response.status_code, response.text)

404 <h1>Not found: /videos/missing</h1>



not_found(template_file='errors/404.pt', **data) renders the page with status 404.
error(template_file, status_code=500, **data) renders any error page.
generic_error(template_file, status_code, template_data) is fastapi-chameleon’s name for error().

They raise chameleon_rs.web.NotFound and chameleon_rs.web.ErrorPage, which the decorator turns into the response.






WarningTemplate names come from your code



The names given to @template, render(), response(), not_found() / error() and render_partial() are looked up as the original libraries look them up, which allows .. and absolute paths. Write them in your code; never build one from a request (a path or query parameter, a header). chameleon_rs.starlette.Templates, the Jinja drop-in, refuses names that reach outside its folder, as Jinja does.




Rendering without the decorator
html = chameleon_flask.render('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)            # a str
resp = chameleon_flask.response('feed.pt', content_type='application/xml', items=items)
render() and response() work anywhere, such as in a view that builds its own response or in a background job. Both raise FlaskChameleonException if nothing has been configured.


One configuration per app
Pass app= to give one Flask or Quart app its own template folder. It’s stored in app.extensions['chameleon_rs'] and used while that app handles a request. Other apps, and code outside a request, use the process-wide configuration. It also turns on the decorator-order check for that app.
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder='admin/templates', app=admin_app)


Quart
The same module works with Quart, with no extra install:
import quart

import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

app = quart.Quart(__name__)
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=template_folder)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
async def index():
    videos = await load_videos()
    return {'message': 'Hello', 'videos': videos}
An async view’s page renders with render_async: a model value that is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future) is awaited where the template uses it, without blocking the event loop. With no awaitable values the output is the same as render()’s.


Coming from chameleon-flask







chameleon-flask
chameleon-rs




global_init(folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True)
Still works. It configures the views only, as before, and ignores a second call. configure() sets views and partials together, and every call applies.


@template, render, response, not_found
Same. not_found also takes the template as template_file=, as well as four04template_file=.


—
error(), any status code.


FlaskChameleonException, FlaskChameleonNotFoundException
Same, now subclasses of chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError and NotFound. except chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError catches them all.


Views return a dict
Also mappings, dataclasses and Pydantic models.

title: Switching from Chameleon
text: chameleon-rs runs code written for Chameleon unchanged. There are two ways to switch: install the compatibility alias and change nothing else, or change your imports.

title: Switching from Chameleon
section: Keep the original chameleon_partials or chameleon-flask
text:
Keep the original chameleon_partials or chameleon-flask
install(integrations=False) maps only chameleon. chameleon_partials and chameleon_flask then import the original packages, which still render through chameleon-rs’s engine. Use it if you depend on behaviour of those packages that the built-ins don’t copy. A chameleon_partials.render_partial from the original package, passed into a template, still renders natively.

title: Getting started
Partials
text:
A partial is a template file rendered inside another template, with its own small model. Use them for anything you repeat: a card in a listing, a form field, a table row, a fragment you also return on its own to HTMX.
chameleon-rs has partials built in. Every template can call render_partial, with nothing to register or pass in:
render_partial(path, **kwargs) renders the template at path with kwargs as its variables, and inserts the result unescaped. Written as a whole ${...} expression, as above, it doesn’t make a Python call at all: the partial renders as a native frame of the page. That makes a listing of partials about 10x faster than Chameleon with chameleon_partials.

title: Partials
text:
chameleon_partials’ lookup: partial_search='registered'
chameleon_partials resolves every path against the registered folder only, and treats any other path as an error. To get exactly that behaviour:
chameleon_rs.configure(partial_search='registered')
The default only differs from chameleon_partials where chameleon_partials would raise, so templates that work there work the same way here.

title: FastAPI
text:
chameleon_rs.fastapi renders templates from FastAPI views. It has fastapi-chameleon’s API, so moving an app over is an import change, or no change at all with chameleon_rs.compat.install() (which makes import fastapi_chameleon give this module).
import chameleon_rs doesn’t import FastAPI. Only import chameleon_rs.fastapi does. There is nothing extra to install: it uses the FastAPI your app already has.

A first view

import fastapi
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode, app=app)


@app.get('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def index(limit: int = 2):
    videos = ['intro', 'partials', 'async']
    return {'message': 'Hello', 'videos': videos[:limit]}

The view returns the template’s model, and @template renders it into a fastapi.Response (text/html):

with TestClient(app) as client:
    print(client.get('/?limit=1').text)
    print(client.get('/?limit=lots').status_code)   # FastAPI's own validation

<h1>Hello</h1>
<ul><li><a href="/videos/intro">intro</a></li></ul>
422


The decorated view keeps its signature, so path and query parameters, Depends, validation errors and the OpenAPI docs are exactly what they would be without @template.
configure() here is the same call as chameleon_rs.configure(), so it also tells render_partial where templates live. app= turns on the decorator-order check below.


Decorator order
@template goes below the route decorator. Written above it, FastAPI registers the bare view, the template never renders and the route quietly returns the view’s dict as JSON. An app given to configure(..., app=app) checks this when it starts:

bad = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.configure(app=bad)
router = fastapi.APIRouter()


@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')   # wrong: above the route
@router.get('/about')
def about():
    return {'message': 'About', 'videos': []}


bad.include_router(router)

try:
    with TestClient(bad):
        pass
except Exception as error:
    print(type(error).__name__)
    print(str(error).split(' at ')[0])

DecoratorOrderError
@template must be placed below the route decorator (@app.get, @router.get, @app.api_route, ...) on about()


The check runs inside the app’s lifespan startup, so Uvicorn and Granian report a failed startup and exit. When no lifespan runs (a server with lifespan events off, a test client used without with, a mounted sub-application) it runs before the first request instead. Routers included with include_router and mounted apps are checked too. A function registered raw on purpose (say, JSON on one route) and also decorated on another route is not flagged. fastapi_chameleon.check_views(app) runs the same check on demand.
One pattern can’t be told from the mistake: a function routed raw on this app whose @template wrapper is used somewhere else (called from another view, or routed on another app). For such an app, pass check_order=False to configure() and keep the check in a test with fastapi_chameleon.check_views(app, ignore=[that_function]).


Sync and async views

An async def view renders its page with render_async on the event loop. A model value that is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future) is awaited where the template uses it, so a slow query can be handed to the template unawaited.
A plain def view renders with render(). FastAPI runs the view, render included, in its thread pool, as with fastapi-chameleon.

@template(..., concurrent=True) renders render_partial(...) calls with awaitable arguments concurrently; @template(..., offload=True) (experimental) renders in a worker thread.
The template gets what the view returns, and nothing else: unlike chameleon_rs.starlette’s endpoints, a FastAPI view’s template does not get request or url_for added, as with fastapi-chameleon (a FastAPI view has no request unless it declares one). Return them in the model if the template needs them.


What a view can return

A model: a dict, any other mapping, a dataclass instance (its fields, shallowly) or a Pydantic model (anything with a callable model_dump()).
A response: any Starlette response (fastapi.Response, RedirectResponse, JSONResponse, …) passes through unchanged.

Anything else raises chameleon_rs.fastapi.FastAPIChameleonException.


The @template decorator
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')                   # a template path
@fastapi_chameleon.template('feed.pt', 'application/xml')      # mimetype=, or content_type=
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/created.pt', status_code=201)
@fastapi_chameleon.template                                    # no arguments
With no path, it renders {module}/{function}.html, where {module} is the last part of the view’s module name. If there’s no .html file in the template folder, it uses {module}/{function}.pt. It checks once, when the view is decorated.


Error pages
Inside a decorated view, not_found() and error() stop the view and render an error page:

app = fastapi.FastAPI()


@app.get('/videos/{name}')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def video(name: str, request: fastapi.Request):
    if name != 'intro':
        fastapi_chameleon.not_found(path=request.url.path)   # renders errors/404.pt
    return {'message': name, 'videos': [name]}


response = TestClient(app).get('/videos/missing')
print(response.status_code, response.text)

404 <h1>Not found: /videos/missing</h1>



not_found(template_file='errors/404.pt', **data) renders the page with status 404.
error(template_file, status_code=500, **data) renders any error page.
generic_error(template_file, status_code, template_data) is fastapi-chameleon’s name and signature for error().







WarningTemplate names come from your code



The names given to @template, render(), response(), not_found() / error() and render_partial() are looked up as the original libraries look them up, which allows .. and absolute paths. Write them in your code; never build one from a request (a path or query parameter, a header). chameleon_rs.starlette.Templates, the Jinja drop-in, refuses names that reach outside its folder, as Jinja does.




Rendering without the decorator
html = fastapi_chameleon.render('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)        # a str
html = await fastapi_chameleon.render_async('emails/welcome.pt', user=user)
resp = fastapi_chameleon.response('feed.pt', 'application/xml', items=items)
resp = await fastapi_chameleon.response_async('feed.pt', status_code=201, items=items)
Both raise FastAPIChameleonException if nothing has been configured.


Coming from fastapi-chameleon







fastapi-chameleon
chameleon-rs




global_init(folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True)
Still works, and takes app=. It configures the views only, as before, and ignores a second call. configure() sets views and partials together, and every call applies.


@template(file, mimetype), render, response, not_found, generic_error
Same. @template also takes status_code= and content_type=; not_found also takes template_file= and template data.


—
error(), render_async(), response_async(), check_views().


FastAPIChameleonException and the not-found / generic exceptions
Same names, now subclasses of chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError, NotFound and ErrorPage.


Views return a dict
Also mappings, dataclasses and Pydantic models.


Async views render synchronously
They render with render_async; an awaitable model value is awaited where the template uses it.



Settings are process-wide. Unlike Flask, a FastAPI app can’t have a template folder of its own yet: the decorator has no request to find the app from.

title: Starlette
text:
chameleon_rs.starlette renders templates from Starlette endpoints, two ways:
import chameleon_rs doesn’t import Starlette. Only import chameleon_rs.starlette does, and it uses the Starlette your app already has (1.x, and 0.46 or later).

title: Starlette
text:
Differences from older Starlette
Starlette 1.x’s signature is the one implemented, request first. On Starlette 0.46 and later 0.x, Jinja2Templates also accepts the old TemplateResponse(name, {'request': request}) form with a DeprecationWarning; Templates raises a TypeError saying the request comes first. And 0.x adds request to a context={} you pass in (1.x, and Templates, give an empty context a new dict, leaving yours untouched).

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Adapted from Chameleon’s language reference (source), modified for chameleon-rs. Used under Chameleon’s license; see LICENSE.txt and COPYRIGHT.txt in the repository.
The Macro Expansion Template Attribute Language (METAL) standard is a facility for HTML/XML macro preprocessing. It can be used in conjunction with or independently of TAL and TALES.
Macros provide a way to define a chunk of presentation in one template, and share it in others, so that changes to the macro are immediately reflected in all of the places that share it. Additionally, macros are always fully expanded, even in a template’s source text, so that the template appears very similar to its final rendering.
A single Page Template can accommodate multiple macros.

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Syntax
metal:define-macro syntax:
argument ::= Name

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Description
The metal:define-macro statement defines a macro. The macro is named by the statement expression, and is defined as the element and its sub-tree.

title: Macros (METAL)
Macros (METAL)
text:
Syntax
metal:define-slot syntax:
argument ::= Name

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Description
The metal:define-slot statement defines a macro customization point or slot. When a macro is used, its slots can be replaced, in order to customize the macro. Slot definitions provide default content for the slot. You will get the default slot contents if you decide not to customize the macro when using it.
The metal:define-slot statement must be used inside a metal:define-macro statement.
Slot names must be unique within a macro.

title: Macros (METAL)
Macros (METAL)
text:
Syntax
metal:fill-slot syntax:
argument ::= Name

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Description
The metal:fill-slot statement customizes a macro by replacing a slot in the macro with the statement element (and its content).
The metal:fill-slot statement must be used inside a metal:use-macro statement.
Slot names must be unique within a macro.
If the named slot does not exist within the macro, the slot contents will be silently dropped.

title: Macros (METAL)
Macros (METAL)
text:
Syntax
metal:use-macro syntax:
argument ::= expression

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Description
The metal:use-macro statement replaces the statement element with a macro. The statement expression describes a macro definition. While the macro runs, the macroname variable is bound to the name it was called with: the use-macro expression as written, after its last / (for container['master.html'].macros.hello that is the whole expression text).






Note



In Chameleon the expression may point to a template instance; in this case it will be rendered in its entirety.

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Syntax
metal:extend-macro syntax:
argument ::= expression

title: Macros (METAL)
text:
Description
To extend an existing macro, choose a name for the macro and add a define-macro attribute to a document element with the name as the argument. Add an extend-macro attribute to the document element with an expression referencing the base macro as the argument. The extend-macro must be used in conjunction with define-macro, and must not be used with use-macro. The element’s subtree is the macro body.

title: Macros (METAL)
Language reference
text:
Adapted from Chameleon’s language reference (source), modified for chameleon-rs. Used under Chameleon’s license; see LICENSE.txt and COPYRIGHT.txt in the repository.



chameleon-rs uses Chameleon’s template language unchanged. This reference can be read as a general introduction to the page templates language. It’s split into parts that correspond to the main language features:



Page
What it covers




Basics (TAL)
The statements that define variables, test conditions, repeat, replace and omit elements, and set attributes.


Expressions (TALES)
The expression types (python, string, exists, not, import, load, structure) and the built-in names.


Macros (METAL)
Defining, using and extending macros, and filling their slots.


Translation (I18N)
The i18n namespace, translation functions and message extraction.


Inline syntax
The ${...} operator, <?python ?> code blocks and markup comments.


Extensions and differences
What Chameleon adds to the page templates language, and how it differs from Zope’s.




Syntax
You can safely skip this section if you’re familiar with how template languages work or just want to learn by example.
An attribute language is a programming language designed to render documents written in XML or HTML markup. The input must be a well-formed document. The output from the template is usually XML-like but isn’t required to be well-formed.
The statements of the language are document tags with special attributes, and look like this:
<p namespace-prefix:command="argument"> ... </p>
In the above example, the attribute namespace-prefix:command="argument" is the statement, and the entire paragraph tag is the statement’s element. The statement’s element is the portion of the document on which this statement operates.
The namespace prefixes are typically declared once, at the top of a template (note that prefix declarations for the template language namespaces are omitted from the template output):
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml"
      xmlns:tal="http://xml.zope.org/namespaces/tal"
      xmlns:metal="http://xml.zope.org/namespaces/metal"
      xmlns:i18n="http://xml.zope.org/namespaces/i18n">
  ...
</html>
Thankfully, sane namespace prefix defaults are in place to let us skip most of the boilerplate:
<html xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1999/xhtml">
  <body>
    <p tal:content="text"> ... </p>
  </body>
</html>
Note how tal is used without an explicit namespace declaration. Chameleon sets up defaults for metal and i18n as well.






Note



Default prefixes are a special feature of Chameleon.


If the enable_data_attributes option is set then you can use data-prefix-command="argument" in addition to the namespace prefix attributes:
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

template = PageTemplate('<p data-tal-content="text">...</p>', enable_data_attributes=True)


chameleon-rs and this reference
Every statement, expression type and built-in name described here behaves in chameleon-rs as it does in Chameleon; the examples on these pages were rendered with both engines to check. The engine underneath is different, which shows in three places, none of them in the template language itself:

Chameleon compiles a template to Python source code, available as template.source. chameleon-rs compiles it to a native program; with keep_source=True, template.source is a readable dump of that program, not Python code.
Custom expression types (classes that return Python AST) work through a bridge, at the speed of an ordinary Python call. Types that depend on Chameleon’s compiler internals beyond that interface aren’t supported.
Chameleon’s CHAMELEON_CACHE (compiled templates cached on disk as Python modules) has no equivalent. Compiling is fast enough that it isn’t needed.

See Compatibility for how compatibility is measured.

title: Expressions (TALES)
text:
Adapted from Chameleon’s language reference (source), modified for chameleon-rs. Used under Chameleon’s license; see LICENSE.txt and COPYRIGHT.txt in the repository.
The Template Attribute Language Expression Syntax (TALES) standard describes expressions that supply TAL and METAL with data. TALES is one possible expression syntax for these languages, but they are not bound to this definition. Similarly, TALES could be used in a context having nothing to do with TAL or METAL.
TALES expressions are described below with any delimiter or quote markup from higher language layers removed. Here is the basic definition of TALES syntax:
Here are some simple examples:
The optional type prefix determines the semantics and syntax of the expression string that follows it. A given implementation of TALES can define any number of expression types, with whatever syntax you like. It also determines which expression type is indicated by omitting the prefix.

Python expression syntax:
Any valid Python language expression

title: Expressions (TALES)
text:
Description
Python expressions are executed natively within the template. There is no built-in security apparatus.






Note



chameleon-rs: Chameleon translates the whole template, expressions included, into Python source code. chameleon-rs compiles the template into a native program; each expression is either evaluated by a native fast path with the same semantics or compiled by CPython. Either way it’s ordinary Python, with access to everything in scope.

title: Expressions (TALES)
text:
Syntax
String expression syntax:
string_expression ::= ( plain_string | [ varsub ] )*
varsub            ::= ( '$' Variable ) | ( '${ Expression }' )
plain_string      ::= ( '$$' | non_dollar )*
non_dollar        ::= any character except '$'

title: Expressions (TALES)
text:
Description
String expressions interpret the expression string as text. If no expression string is supplied the resulting string is empty. The string can contain variable substitutions of the form $name or ${expression}, where name is a variable name, and expression is a TALES-expression. The escaped string value of the expression is inserted into the string.






Note



To prevent a $ from being interpreted this way, it must be escaped as $$. Using a backslash-escape is not supported.

Translation (I18N)
text:
Adapted from Chameleon’s language reference (source), modified for chameleon-rs. Used under Chameleon’s license; see LICENSE.txt and COPYRIGHT.txt in the repository.
Translation of template contents and attributes is supported via the i18n namespace and message objects.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:translate
This attribute is used to mark units of text for translation. If this attribute is specified with an empty string as the value, the message ID is computed from the content of the element bearing this attribute. Otherwise, the value of the element gives the message ID.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:domain
The i18n:domain attribute is used to specify the domain to be used to get the translation. If not specified, the translation services will use a default domain. The value of the attribute is used directly; it is not a TALES expression.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:context
The i18n:context attribute is used to specify the context to be used to get the translation. If not specified, the translation services will use a default context. The context is generally used to distinguish identical texts in different contexts (because in a translation this may not be the case). The value of the attribute is used literally; it is not an expression.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:source
The i18n:source attribute specifies the language of the text to be translated. The default is nothing, which means we don’t provide this information to the translation services.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:target
The i18n:target attribute specifies the language of the translation we want to get. If the value is default, the language negotiation services will be used to choose the destination language. If the value is nothing, no translation will be performed; this can be used to suppress translation within a larger translated unit. Any other value must be a language code.
The attribute value is a TALES expression; the result of evaluating the expression is the language code or one of the reserved values.






Note



i18n:target is primarily used for hints to text extraction tools and translation teams. If you had some text that should only be translated to e.g. German, then it probably shouldn’t be wrapped in an i18n:translate span.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:name
Name the content of the current element for use in interpolation within translated content. This allows a replaceable component in content to be re-ordered by translation. For example:
<span i18n:translate=''>
  <span tal:replace='context.name' i18n:name='name' /> was born in
  <span tal:replace='context.country_of_birth' i18n:name='country' />.
</span>
would cause this text to be passed to the translation service:
"${name} was born in ${country}."

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:attributes
This attribute will allow us to translate attributes of HTML tags, such as the alt attribute in the img tag. The i18n:attributes attribute specifies a list of attributes to be translated with optional message IDs for each; if multiple attribute names are given, they must be separated by semicolons. Message IDs used in this context must not include whitespace.
Note that the value of the particular attributes come either from the HTML attribute value itself or from the data inserted by tal:attributes.
If an attribute is to be both computed using tal:attributes and translated, the translation service is passed the result of the TALES expression for that attribute.
An example:
<img src="http://foo.com/logo" alt="Visit us"
     tal:attributes="alt context.greeting"
     i18n:attributes="alt"
     >
In this example, we let tal:attributes set the value of the alt attribute to the text “Stop by for a visit!”. This text will be passed to the translation service, which uses the result of language negotiation to translate “Stop by for a visit!” into the requested language. The example text in the template, “Visit us”, will simply be discarded.
Another example, with explicit message IDs:
<img src="../icons/uparrow.png" alt="Up"
     i18n:attributes="src up-arrow-icon; alt up-arrow-alttext"
     >
Here, the message ID up-arrow-icon will be used to generate the link to an icon image file, and the message ID ‘up-arrow-alttext’ will be used for the “alt” text.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:data
Since TAL always returns strings, we need a way in ZPT to translate objects, one of the most obvious cases being datetime objects. The data attribute will allow us to specify such an object, and i18n:translate will provide us with a legal format string for that object. If data is used, i18n:translate must be used to give an explicit message ID, rather than relying on a message ID computed from the content.

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:comment
The i18n:comment attribute can be used to add extra comments for translators. It is not used by Chameleon for processing, but will be picked up by tools like lingua.
An example:
<h3 i18n:comment="Header for the news section"
    i18n:translate="">News</h3>

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:ignore
The i18n:ignore attribute can be used to inform translation extraction tools like i18ndude to not give a warning/error on the given tag if there is no i18n:translate attribute.
An example:
<h1 i18n:ignore="">News</h1>

title: Translation (I18N)
text:
i18n:ignore-attributes
The i18n:ignore-attributes, just like i18n:ignore is expected to be used by translation extraction tools like i18ndude. If i18n:ignore makes text within a tag to be ignored, i18n:ignore-attributes marks the given attributes as ignored.
An example:
<a href="http://python.org"
   title="Python!"
   i18n:ignore-attributes="title">Python website</a>

title: Testing templates with pytest
text:
Every template compiles
A typo in a TAL attribute or an expression is a compile error. Chameleon compiles a template when it’s first rendered, so a broken template can go unnoticed until someone opens that page. This test compiles all of them:
# tests/test_templates_compile.py
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateFile

TEMPLATES = Path(__file__).parent.parent / 'myapp' / 'templates'


@pytest.mark.parametrize('path', sorted(TEMPLATES.rglob('*.pt')), ids=str)
def test_template_compiles(path):
    PageTemplateFile(str(path)).cook_check()
cook_check() compiles without rendering, so the test needs no model. chameleon-rs compiles in about 0.05 ms per template, so even a few hundred templates take well under a second.
The CHAMELEON_EAGER=1 environment variable does the same at load time: file templates then compile as soon as they’re created.


Test the rendered output
Render a partial with the model your view would pass, and assert on the HTML:
import chameleon_rs


@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)
def templates():
    chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=str(TEMPLATES))
    yield
    chameleon_rs.partials.clear()


def test_video_card_shows_title():
    html = chameleon_rs.render_partial('shared/video_card.pt', video=Video(1, 'Intro')).html_text
    assert '<a href="/videos/1">Intro</a>' in html
The fixture’s clear() forgets the configuration, so tests that configure a different folder don’t leak into each other.
For a Flask app, use its test client. See HTMX fragments for an example.


Compare against Chameleon
While you’re migrating, a test can render the same template with both engines and compare. Install stock Chameleon in the test environment only:
import chameleon
import chameleon_rs


def test_same_output_as_chameleon():
    path = str(TEMPLATES / 'home' / 'index.pt')
    model = {'title': 'Home', 'videos': []}
    assert chameleon_rs.PageTemplateFile(path)(**model) == chameleon.PageTemplateFile(path)(**model)
On a running staging app, shadow mode does this for every render.

# chameleon-rs

Chameleon templates, modernized: a Rust engine that runs Chameleon templates unchanged, several times faster, with async rendering and built-in framework integrations.

## Installation

```bash
pip install chameleon-rs
```

## When to use what

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| Run an existing Chameleon app on chameleon-rs with no code changes | `chameleon_rs.compat.install() at the top of the entry point` |
| Render a template string | `chameleon_rs.PageTemplate(source)(**model)` |
| Load templates by name from folders | `chameleon_rs.PageTemplateLoader([folder])['page.pt'](**model)` |
| Insert a reusable HTML fragment | `${render_partial('shared/fragment.pt', key=value)}` |
| Get a rendered fragment as a string from Python (HTMX, email, tests) | `chameleon_rs.render_partial(path, **model).html_text` |
| Render Chameleon templates from Flask or Quart views | `chameleon_rs.flask: configure(folder), then @template('page.pt') on the view` |
| Render Chameleon templates from FastAPI views | `chameleon_rs.fastapi: configure(folder, app=app), then @template('page.pt') below @app.get` |
| Replace Starlette's Jinja2Templates | `chameleon_rs.starlette.Templates(directory=folder); await templates.TemplateResponse_async(request, 'page.pt', context) in async endpoints` |
| Render Chameleon templates from Robyn handlers | `chameleon_rs.robyn: configure(folder, app=app), then @template('page.pt') below @app.get (Robyn has wheels for Python 3.10-3.14)` |
| Render without blocking the event loop | `await template.render_async(**model); in the framework integrations, an async def view with @template does this` |
| Run several slow async helpers of one page at the same time | `@chameleon_rs.concurrent on the helper, called as a whole ${helper(...)}; or PageTemplate(..., concurrent=True) / @template(..., concurrent=True) for partials with awaitable arguments` |
| Convert Markdown to HTML in a template | `chameleon_rs.configure(markdown=True), then ${markdown: post.body}; profiles such as {'md-trusted': {'raw_html': 'allow'}} for different content` |
| Render Chameleon templates from Pyramid views | `pyramid_chameleon unchanged (config.include('pyramid_chameleon'), renderer='templates/page.pt'), with chameleon_rs.compat.install() before it is imported` |
| Use Chameleon templates as Litestar's template engine | `TemplateConfig(engine=chameleon_rs.litestar.ChameleonEngine, directory=folder); return chameleon_rs.litestar.Template('page.pt', context=...) (served as text/html; renders synchronously)` |
| Render Chameleon templates from async Litestar handlers without blocking the loop | `chameleon_rs.litestar: configure(folder, app=app), then @template('page.pt') below @get` |

## API overview

### Templates

- `PageTemplateFile`: File-based constructor: the template is read from ``filename`` (or, with
- `PageTextTemplate`: Text-based template class: only ``${...}`` interpolation, no markup, nothing escaped
- `PageTextTemplateFile`: File-based text template. Rendering returns ``bytes``, encoded with the template's

### Async

### Partials

## Gotchas

1. chameleon_rs.compat.install() must run before anything imports chameleon, chameleon_partials, chameleon_flask, fastapi_chameleon or chameleon_robyn; a module already imported keeps stock Chameleon's objects.
2. render_partial looks in the configured template folder, then on the calling template's search path and in its folder and each folder above it. chameleon_rs.configure(partial_search='registered') restores chameleon_partials' lookup (configured folder only).
3. render_partial is a builtin in every template; you don't need extend_model() or a BeforeRender subscriber (both still work).
4. configure() applies on every call (there is no cache_init); the first call must give template_folder.
5. template.source does not exist as Python code: with keep_source=True it is a dump of the compiled program.
6. Custom expression types that return Python AST work through a bridge at fallback speed; types that depend on Chameleon's compiler internals are not supported.
7. render_async awaits only an expression's final value: ${episodes} and tal:repeat="e episodes" await a coroutine, ${episodes.count} and ${len(episodes)} do not.
8. markdown: expressions exist only after chameleon_rs.configure(markdown=True) (or a dict of profiles), called before the templates that use them compile.
9. Pyramid has no chameleon_rs module: pyramid_chameleon runs unchanged after chameleon_rs.compat.install() at the top of the package whose main() builds the app.

## Best practices

- Call chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=..., auto_reload=dev_mode) once at startup, before the first render.
- To switch an existing app, add `import chameleon_rs.compat; chameleon_rs.compat.install()` as the first lines of the entry point, and leave the rest of the code unchanged.
- Prefer ${render_partial('shared/card.pt', item=item)} as a whole expression: it renders as a native frame of the page, with no Python call.
- Build template folder paths with (Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix().
- In tests, reset with chameleon_rs.partials.clear() (or chameleon_rs.flask.clear(), chameleon_rs.fastapi.clear(), chameleon_rs.starlette.clear(), chameleon_rs.robyn.clear(), chameleon_rs.litestar.clear()) between configurations.
- Put @template below the route decorator (@app.get, @router.get, @app.route, Litestar's @get); pass app= to configure() so a misordered view fails at startup with DecoratorOrderError.
- With Litestar, return chameleon_rs.litestar.Template (not litestar.response.Template) for .pt templates: Litestar guesses the media type from the suffix and serves .pt as text/plain.

## What chameleon-rs is

Chameleon's template language on a new engine written in Rust (`import chameleon_rs`, PyPI
`chameleon-rs`). Same template language (TAL, METAL, i18n, `${...}`), same Python API, the
same output byte for byte, several times faster. It adds async rendering (`render_async`),
built-in Flask/Quart, FastAPI, Starlette, Robyn and Litestar integrations, built-in partials,
`markdown:` expressions, and free-threaded Python support. It has no runtime dependencies, and
stock Chameleon doesn't need to be installed.

## Switching an existing Chameleon app

Add these lines at the very top of the app's entry point, above every other import:

```python
import chameleon_rs.compat

chameleon_rs.compat.install()
```

After that, `import chameleon`, `import chameleon_partials`, `import chameleon_flask`,
`import fastapi_chameleon` and `import chameleon_robyn` give chameleon-rs's modules. Don't change templates or other code. If `chameleon` was imported
before `install()`, objects taken from it stay stock Chameleon objects, so move the call
earlier.

## A new app

```python
from pathlib import Path

import chameleon_rs
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateLoader

folder = (Path(__file__).parent / 'templates').as_posix()
chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)  # once, at startup
templates = PageTemplateLoader([folder])

html = templates['home/index.pt'](title='Home', videos=videos)
```

Every template has `render_partial` built in, with no `extend_model` and no `BeforeRender`
subscriber:

```html
<div tal:repeat="video videos">
  ${render_partial('shared/video_card.pt', video=video)}
</div>
```

A partial sees only the keyword arguments passed to it. A path is looked for in the
configured folder, then next to the calling template and in the folders above it.

## Flask and Quart

```python
import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)

@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
def index():
    return {'message': 'Hello'}   # a dict, mapping, dataclass or Pydantic model
```

`chameleon_flask.not_found()` and `chameleon_flask.error(template, status_code)` end a
decorated view with an error page. `chameleon_rs.render_partial(path, **model).html_text`
returns a fragment as a string, for HTMX responses.

## Other frameworks

`chameleon_rs.fastapi`, `chameleon_rs.starlette`, `chameleon_rs.robyn` and
`chameleon_rs.litestar` have the same decorator API (`configure(template_folder=..., app=app)`,
`@template('page.pt')` below the route decorator, `not_found`, `error`, `render`, `response`,
`render_async`, `response_async`). Also:

- Starlette: `chameleon_rs.starlette.Templates(directory=...)` is a drop-in for
  `Jinja2Templates`; use `await templates.TemplateResponse_async(request, name, context)` in
  async endpoints.
- Litestar: `TemplateConfig(engine=chameleon_rs.litestar.ChameleonEngine, directory=...)`, and
  return `chameleon_rs.litestar.Template` (serves `.pt` as `text/html`).
- Pyramid: no module; pyramid_chameleon runs unchanged after `chameleon_rs.compat.install()`.

## Async rendering

`await template.render_async(**model)` awaits an awaitable model value (coroutine, task,
future) where the template uses it, without blocking the event loop. Only an expression's final
value is awaited: `${episodes}` and `tal:repeat="e episodes"` await, `${episodes.count}` does
not. An `async def` view with `@template` renders this way in every integration. Opt-in:
`@chameleon_rs.concurrent` helpers and `concurrent=True` partials run concurrently.

## Markdown

```python
chameleon_rs.configure(markdown=True)   # at startup, before templates compile
```

```html
<article>${markdown: post.body}</article>
```

Raw HTML in the text is escaped by default; a profile such as
`configure(markdown={'markdown': {}, 'md-trusted': {'raw_html': 'allow'}})` adds an
`md-trusted:` prefix for trusted content.

## Known differences from Chameleon

- `template.source` is a dump of the compiled program, not Python code.
- Custom expression types that return Python AST work through a bridge, at the speed of an
  ordinary Python call.
- `CHAMELEON_CACHE` writes nothing to disk; compiling is fast enough not to need it.
- `chameleon.nodes`, `chameleon.program`, `chameleon.zpt.program` and `chameleon.benchmark`
  don't exist.

Usage

fastapi.template(template_file: Callable[P, Coroutine[Any, Any, Any]]) -> Callable[P, Coroutine[Any, Any, fastapi.Response]]

fastapi.template(template_file: str | None = None, mimetype: str = 'text/html', status_code: int = 200, content_type: str | None = None, concurrent: bool | None = None, offload: bool = False) -> TemplateDecorator

The same as render, except that when an expression’s final value is awaitable (a coroutine, a task, a future, anything await accepts), the render suspends until the value is awaited and continues with its result. Values inside an expression are not awaited (coro().title is the coroutine’s attribute), and a condition is tested on the awaited value. An error raised by an awaited value is raised where the expression is, so tal:on-error handles it; cancellation passes through.
Opt-in concurrency: calls of @chameleon_rs.concurrent helpers written as a whole ${...} are awaited concurrently, and with the template setting concurrent=True native partials called with an awaitable argument render concurrently (see chameleon_rs._async).
Experimental, opt-in: offload=True runs render (synchronous: awaitable values are not awaited) in the event loop’s default executor, a worker thread, and awaits it. On a free-threaded build renders then run in parallel with the event loop and each other; on a GIL build it helps only renders dominated by long text, whose escaping releases the GIL (docs/plan.md, Phase 11 results). offload is therefore not a template variable here.

title: shadow.install()
text:
Starts shadow mode: from now on, a sample_rate share of the outermost renders of


Usage
Source


shadow.install(
    *, serve="chameleon", sample_rate=1.0, report=None, log_interval=600.0
)


stock Chameleon page templates also renders with chameleon-rs (doubling their latency: keep it well below 1 on real traffic), and the application gets the outcome (output or exception) of the serve engine. Differences go to report (default: a capped warning on the chameleon_rs.shadow logger, once per distinct difference per log_interval seconds). Calling it again replaces the settings.
